claims.text: Integrating phase-field simulations with CALPHAD assessments during thermal processing can enable controlled phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
Thermal processing guided by the integrated framework can tune the free-energy landscape to favor desired constituent phases.
The initial Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA contains a mixture of constituent phases and precursors to multiple phase transformations.
The proposed intervention is annealing and controlled cooling using parameters optimized through an integrated phase-field and CALPHAD framework.
Annealing temperature, dwell time, and cooling rate can be selected from computational predictions to control processing.
The free-energy landscape and phase-specific nucleation and growth pathways mediate phase evolution.
CALPHAD uses phase Gibbs energies as functions of pressure, temperature, and composition and calculates equilibrium by energy minimization.
Combining phase-field simulations with CALPHAD maps both thermodynamic and kinetic pathways.
Adjusting thermal parameters through the framework can specifically modulate transformation-energy barriers.
Modulation of transformation-energy barriers can tailor phase nucleation and growth rates.
The intervention will produce a targeted balance of FCC, BCC, or other ordered phases.
The targeted phase balance will improve the consistency and overall properties of the alloy.
Conventional thermal processing without computational guidance causes less predictable phase evolution and greater microstructural heterogeneity.
The method's efficacy depends on the accuracy of its thermodynamic databases.
The method's efficacy depends on the accuracy of kinetic parameters used in the simulations.
Experimental inability to reproduce computed thermal histories may limit the method's efficacy.
The achievable degree of phase control and the quantitative mechanical-property effects remain uncertain and require experimental validation.
Phase distributions and microstructural uniformity can be compared between conventionally processed samples and simulation-optimized samples.
XRD, SEM, and TEM can measure phase identity, microstructure, and phase-boundary characteristics relevant to the proposed outcome.
Failure of optimized processing to produce statistically significant improvements over conventional processing would falsify the hypothesis.
